inline.s: 31. Bestowing kindness without seeking repayment; giving to others without afterward regretting it.
32. What is meant by a good man.
33. All people revere him; Heaven’s Way protects him; blessings and emoluments follow him; every evil influence withdraws from him; gods and spirits guard him.
34. Whatever he undertakes must succeed; the state of the immortals may be hoped for.
35. One who seeks to become a celestial immortal must establish one thousand three hundred good deeds; one who seeks to become an earthly immortal must establish three hundred good deeds.
36. Acting without righteousness, and walking contrary to reason.
37. Taking evil for ability.
38. Hardening the heart to do harm.
39. Secretly injuring the good and virtuous; covertly insulting ruler and parents.
40. Treating one’s teacher with disrespect; betraying those one serves.
41. Deceiving the ignorant; slandering one’s fellow students.
42. Falsely accusing others and practicing deceit; attacking and exposing one’s own kinsmen.
43. Being hard and unyielding, without kindness; fierce and self-willed.
44. Judging right and wrong improperly; favoring and opposing where it is unfitting.
45. Oppressing those below to win merit; flattering those above to court their favor.
46. Receiving kindness without gratitude; nursing resentment without ceasing.

Filial piety and fraternal duty are one in root, and the reason they are here spoken of separately is that one would have men fulfill them according to each circumstance. An elder brother’s friendliness is to love and also to respect; a younger brother’s duty is to revere and also to be harmonious. Brothers are of one breath with my own body; these few alone are the hardest to come by in a lifetime. Seen from the parents’ side, they were originally one body: let there be the least division between them, and the parents’ hearts are at once grieved and ill at ease. Therefore when they see us brothers loving one another, the parents’ hearts have a place where affection flows through of itself. Moreover, brothers are called hands and feet: each guards and supports the other, sharing every ache and itch — how could a hand and a foot grasp and wrestle with each other? If one bears in mind that at birth we came from the same parents and are one body, and that bone and flesh are hard to sunder, then no quarrel of temper will be borne to be inflicted, and trifling gains will of themselves be held lightly. The Chan master Fazhao’s verse says: ‘Of one breath and joined branches, each flourishes in its own place; let not a few idle words wound the affection between you. Each time we meet, each time we grow older — how long can we remain brothers? When brothers dwell together, forbearance brings peace; let no dispute arise from a hair’s breadth. Before your eyes children are born and are brothers again — leave a pattern for your sons and grandsons to look upon.’ The Yuan Family’s Precepts for the World says: ‘In loving the younger ones, let not the father and elder brother demand that the younger must obey; in loving the father and elder brother, let not the younger demand that the father and elder brother must be kind. Let each strive to do his own utmost, and the fault of reproaching and expecting will of itself disappear. Strictly forbid maids and concubines to carry words to and fro; as for the private talk of a wife, even if it be spoken from true feeling, do not listen — then the beginnings of estrangement will of themselves be cut off. Men’s temperaments are soft or hard, cautious or unruly, quiet or restless; and when they come to handle affairs, their judgments of right and wrong differ. Let each follow what is suitable, and not insist, because I am right, that others must agree with me — and what quarrelling will remain? Even if there is something crooked, and one cannot bear to stand by and watch, one should only be even-tempered and gentle, and counsel with tact. If it is so, will there be any who do not live in harmony? When men today fall out with their own flesh and blood, there are cases where the cause was utterly slight, yet it cannot be undone — only because, after the falling out, each clings to his anger and will not be the first to yield. If within the family there is one wise and clear-sighted who is willing to suffer loss and is able to swallow his anger first, dealing with the other side in affairs and speaking with him, then each returns the other’s courtesy, and the old affection gradually becomes as it was before. Wang Yangming of the Ming dynasty said: Shun was able to transform Xiang; his secret was simply that he did not see Xiang’s wrong. In my humble view, between flesh and blood one should speak only of feeling, not of principle; to insist on principle wounds the feeling, and to wound the feeling is itself to depart from principle. Someone asked Master Cheng: ‘If I serve my elder brother according to principle and still do not win his glad heart, what then?’ He answered: ‘You need only rouse your reverence and your filial devotion, exhaust your utmost sincerity, and not seek to have your own way — that will do.’ Asked, ‘What is the way to receive a younger brother?’ he said: ‘Exhaust the way of friendliness and love, and nothing more.’
Mr. Shao Yaofu of the Song dynasty wrote in his Song of Filial Piety and Fraternal Love:
Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay. Do not wound your own flesh and blood, nor stir up storms of trouble and dismay.
The grace of parents’ toil is heavy and must be repaid; the love of brothers runs deep — let it never decay. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.

Gongyi kept nine generations under one roof — a thing the ages rarely display; Tian Zhen’s brothers shared one home, and sons and grandsons came in long array. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Thus near and far all praise their harmony, and bless the brothers on their way. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay. With cheerful voice and gentle breath, keep humble, meek, and harmonious every day.

Brothers who share hardship bear a name of special weight; worthy sons and worthy grandsons are honored in their own day. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.

Even bearing rice upon his back can be a meager service to repay; shall one who reads the books fail to rise to high degree one day? Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Zhong You and Chen Ji were both like this in their day. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay. Teach the worthy wives of the house to serve their husband’s parents in the proper way.

Gladly keep the lesson of Mencius’s mother, who moved her dwelling three times away; be sure to read Old Master Zhang’s Song of a Hundred Forbearances, come what may. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.

Filial and fraternal, kind to kin and to those joined by marriage, generous and compassionate; wise and humane, sagely and righteous, in harmony and in the middle way. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
In that day Zengzi and Yang Bo were honored in the selfsame way. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay. Heaven’s season, earth’s advantage, and the concord of men attend them on their way.
Say not that the affairs of the world are always so; alas, how brief a span of life, how short our stay. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
What are the crowding splendors that delight the eye? One household’s peace and joy are worth the whole world’s array. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
How wonderful — the boy who yielded the pears, and the boy who hid the oranges for his mother, lead the way. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay. Time passes by as swiftly as the shuttle flies away.

When the parents are happy at home, sons and grandsons are happy; when brothers are harmonious, the wives of the house are harmonious in their way. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.

A household that hands down filial and fraternal conduct leaves a name that will not decay; what avails a cabinet full of gold and silver, come what may? Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Would you have a fair name handed down through all the ages? Then follow this and walk in the appointed way. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay. At dawn and dusk tend and greet your parents; let not the hours slip away.

A household of filial and fraternal hearts is truly hard to find; a hundred years of time are the easiest to let slip by. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.

In joy and harmony take your delight, and let all draw together; the ordering of human ties rests upon humility and gentle ways. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
The motley robe is danced for the parents’ joy, and ocarina and flute sound out a brotherly concord. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay. Let not a husband heed the whispered promptings of his wife, come what may.

Gold and silk before your eyes — do not complain that there is too little; sons and grandsons at your knee — never tire of their being many. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
If only the family is at peace, poverty is good; if wealth comes by injustice, what is it worth? Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Wang and Han, filial and fraternal, are recorded in the pages of history. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay. Do not wound the household’s harmony with angry brawling day by day.

Those who give way to envy fall the deeper into hardship; those who secretly hoard for themselves are secretly tormented. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
From unfilial conduct rebellious children are born of themselves; from wicked conduct demons and goblins surely come. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Only hear how filial and fraternal conduct is handed down through a thousand ages. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay. Do not, for some trifling thing, suddenly wound the family peace and turn away.

In the golden chest, do not complain that there is too little; of hidden merit in the darkness, lay up as much as you may. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.

How can crooked self-seeking compare with the good of fair dealing? The hard and violent are helpless before the gentle and the good. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
In the records of ancient and modern times, many are the fair names won. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay. Alas for those who split the household and lend an ear to mischief day by day.
Each complains that the money in his purse is too little, and claims too much of the ancestral fields. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
Though husband and wife may be happy for the moment, their sons and grandsons may later be brought to ruin. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.
How much better to be filial and fraternal, and kind to one’s own village and kin. Sons serve their parents, younger brothers revere the elder — so runs the lay.

In the Han dynasty there were three brothers of the Tian family, the eldest named Zhen. They agreed to divide the family property, and shared the assets out equally. Before the hall stood a redbud tree, which they proposed to split into three; the next day, when they were about to cut it, the tree withered. Zhen was startled, and said to his younger brothers: ‘The tree is one trunk. Hearing that it was to be cut apart, it has withered. We men are not the equal of a tree.’ Thereupon his grief overcame him and he would not divide the tree; and at his words the tree came back to life. The brothers were moved, pooled their property, and dwelt together, and their household was called a gate of filial piety. Now brothers hold one of the natural human relations, and with father and son, and husband and wife, they make up the three bonds. Hence the ancients likened them to hands and feet, meaning that they are not to be parted. Parted, they scatter; scattered, each is left alone; alone, they perish.

Sima Guang, Duke Wen, of the Song dynasty had an elder brother, Bokang, who was eighty years old. He served him as he would a stern father, and cherished him as he would an infant. Every time they ate, after a short while he would ask: ‘Are you not hungry?’ And when it grew a little cold, he would stroke his brother’s back and say: ‘Is your clothing not too thin?’

Zhou Wencan was by nature loving and fraternal. His elder brother was given to drink, and depended on Wencan for a living. Once, when drunk, the elder brother beat him, and a neighbor, unable to bear the injustice, cursed the brother. Wencan angrily said: ‘My brother did not beat me. Why do you set my own flesh and blood at odds with me?’

Zheng Degui and Zheng Dezhang of the Song dynasty were filial and fraternal by nature. Their writing tables were joined, and by night they slept under one quilt. Dezhang was upright and firm by temperament, and often came into conflict with others. An enemy framed him on a capital charge, and he was to be arrested at Yangzhou. Degui grieved that his brother should be falsely accused, and said to him with feigned carelessness: ‘It is I they wish to harm — what has it to do with you? If I go, the wicked plot will be made clear. You go, and will you not escape death?’ He at once prepared for the journey. Dezhang pursued and overtook him; the brothers held each other, stamped their feet, and wept, each striving to go and die. Degui secretly contrived to stop the other’s going, and fled away at midnight. Dezhang again pursued him as far as Guangling, but Degui had already died in prison. Dezhang’s grief was such that he swooned away four times. He carried his brother’s bones home for burial, and dwelt in a hut at the grave for two full years. Whenever he wailed in sorrow, crows and other birds gathered circling and would not eat. Degui’s son was young and timid, and Dezhang cherished him as his own child.

Xue Bao of the Han dynasty was fond of learning and earnest in conduct. Hated and driven out by his stepmother, he wept day and night outside the house; at dawn he would go in and sweep and sprinkle the floors, and again she drove him out. So he built a hut at the gate of the village, and morning and evening inquired after his parents’ health. After more than a year his parents came to their senses and called him home. When his parents died, his grief made him ill. His younger brothers asked to live apart; Bao could not hold them back, and let them do as they pleased. Of the servants and maids he took the old and the weak, saying: ‘They have served with me a long time, and are used to my orders.’ Of the vessels and utensils he took the broken and worn ones, saying: ‘These are what I have always used; my body and mouth are at ease with them.’ Of the fields he took the wild and overgrown ones, saying: ‘These I worked in my youth, and my heart clings to them.’ When his younger brothers could not stand on their own and ruined their portion, Bao supplied them again. Emperor An heard of his name and summoned him to be a Palace Attendant, but he would not accept; and he was granted a thousand piculs of grain.

Xu Wu of the Han dynasty was orphaned young, with two younger brothers still small. Wu plowed by day and studied by night. While plowing, though his brothers were too young to hold the hoe, he would have them watch from the side; while studying, he seated them beside him and himself taught them to punctuate and read the text, explaining everything in careful detail, instructing them in propriety and righteousness, and training them to become men. If they were the least disobedient, he would kneel of himself before the ancestral hall, saying that he lacked virtue and could not teach them, and praying that if his parents had any spirit, they would open the eyes of his two brothers; and he would not rise until the two had wailed and begged forgiveness. Never did he meet them with harsh words or an angry face. Though grown to manhood, he did not marry. When someone urged him to, he said: ‘I fear that if I marry the wrong woman, estrangement will easily arise.’ Hence the neighbors called him Xu Wu the filial and fraternal, and the commandery officials all recommended him. He was summoned as a Gentleman Consultant, and his fame spread far. He then hung up his official seals and returned home, and first arranged marriages for his two brothers before marrying himself. They dwelt together in harmony, and in time his brothers’ names became renowned as well.

Niu Hong of the Sui dynasty was Minister of the Board of Personnel. His younger brother Bi, once drunk, shot and killed the ox that drew Hong’s carriage. When Hong returned home, his wife came out to meet him and said: ‘Your brother has shot the ox dead.’ Hong showed no surprise, but quietly answered: ‘Make it into dried meat.’ When they were seated, his wife said again: ‘Your brother has shot the ox dead — it is a monstrous thing.’ Hong said: ‘I know. What is strange about it?’ His countenance was unmoved, and he went on reading without pause. He afterward became a famous minister. When men of the world, in their dealings with brothers, fall out in affection and listen only to the words of their wives — if they see this and do not wake to their senses, are they not beasts?

In the Northern Qi there was a man named Puming. He and his brother quarreled over property and carried on a lawsuit for years, each citing witnesses, until the case came before Su Qiong, governor of Qinghe. Su summoned them and admonished them, saying: ‘In all the world, what is hard to come by is a brother; what is easy to come by is land. Suppose you gain the land and lose your brother — how would your heart feel?’ And he wept. All the witnesses were moved to tears, and the brothers knocked their heads on the ground and yielded to one another.

Yu Tieqiao said: There were two sons of an official of Huaiyin who from childhood were at odds, and for years did not once meet. Later, when the elder brother lay dying, he called his younger brother to his bedside, took his hand, and said: ‘I married at nineteen, so in childhood I had no wife’s love; at thirty-eight I went into mourning, so in my later years I had no parents’ love. Those who were together longest were you and I. Yet all our lives we could not agree. Only now do I repent and wake — and my life is already spent. How bitter!’ Those who hear this may well be moved.

Miao Tong of the Later Han was orphaned young, one of four brothers by different mothers, who held their property in common. When each had taken a wife, the younger brothers asked to divide the household, and quarrels were often heard. Tong shut the door and beat himself, saying: ‘Miao Tong, you cultivate yourself and walk carefully, you study the way of the sages, and you mean to bring order to the customs of the world — how is it that you cannot set your own house in order?’ When his brothers and their wives heard this, they all knocked their heads on the ground and begged forgiveness, and thereafter practiced harmony and affection.

Zhang Shixuan of the Five Dynasties lost his parents in childhood. When he grew up, only his uncle remained. The uncle had seven sons. One day the uncle said to Shixuan: ‘I should divide the property with you, splitting it in two.’ Shixuan said: ‘I cannot bear that seven should share one portion; let it be divided into eight.’ The uncle firmly declined, and Shixuan as firmly yielded, and so it was divided into eight. Shixuan was then seventeen. He was recommended for the capital examinations. With him in the same lodging were more than twenty men. A diviner looked at them and said: ‘Of those who pass high in the examinations of the Southern Palace, only this youth.’ His companions laughed and rebuked him. The diviner said: ‘Letters are not my affair; but this youth’s face is full of the air of hidden virtue, which must come from accumulated good deeds.’ When the list was posted, Shixuan alone took a high place. Now when men make light of the love of brothers and contend for the baseness of goods and wealth — even full brothers of one womb are treated so, while toward half-brothers and the sons of concubines bullying is the more easily bred and the tormenting of one another the fiercer; and as for cousins of the same hall, the more they are divided, the more the degrees of kinship are made to show. Who can be like Master Zhang? They do not know the saying of the ancients: to treat brothers meanly is to treat parents meanly; to treat cousins meanly is to treat ancestors meanly. If the root is injured, the branches and leaves must wither. This is a saying about the very source; men should ponder it three times over.

Mao Lie of the Song dynasty was a friend of Chen Qi. Qi had three young brothers, and fearing that when they grew up the property would be divided, he first privately mortgaged more than half of the fields to Lie, borrowing several thousand strings of cash. After their mother died, only the fields then in hand were divided. More than a year later Qi loaded the money and went to Lie’s house to redeem the land. Lie took the money, but had a mind to swallow it up, and put him off, saying the deed would be given another day. Qi thought that, being an old friend, there could be no trickery. Some days later he came again, and Lie avoided him and would not come out. He brought suit at the county office, but the county had taken Lie’s bribes and said: ‘The magistrate trusts documents; how can one accept that money was paid without a deed?’ Qi ended by being beaten as a false accuser. Afterward he sued again and again, spending almost all of his share of the property, but since the repayment left no evidence, the land remained with Lie. His three younger brothers laughed when they heard of it. Among those in the world who use their seniority to cheat their juniors, is there one who will not meet his own Mao Lie?

There was a man of Jurong who had three brothers: the eldest had gone to Shu on business and had not returned for three years. The second, because his sister-in-law was beautiful, had someone falsely report that the eldest was dead; the widow wept and put on mourning. After a long while, seeing that she had no mind to remarry, he secretly took money from a merchant and sold her to him. He then deceived the merchant, saying: ‘My sister-in-law wishes to marry but is full of false modesty. If you speak fair words, it will take many days. Bring your men and come suddenly; when you see the woman in plain hairpins, seize her and put her in the sedan chair, and only say: “We will talk tomorrow” — and once aboard the boat she is your wife.’ The plan settled, that night the merchant came with his men. The second and third brothers both made themselves scarce, but the third, angry that his share of the silver was small, had already secretly told the widow. The second brother’s wife knew nothing of it. So the widow tearfully told her: ‘Your husband is marrying me off. Fortunately he is a rich merchant. But why did he not tell me earlier, so that I might dress? Now it is a wedding, and can I come in plain dress? Pray lend me your black cap for a moment.’ The second brother’s wife handed it over and put on the plain hairpins herself, whereupon the widow hid herself away. The merchant’s men, seeing the second brother’s wife, carried her off at once; the boat set sail with a fair wind. When the second brother came home, he was astonished to find his wife gone. He chased after, but among a thousand sails in confusion he could not find her. The next morning the eldest brother came home with a heavy pack on his shoulder, and husband and wife were reunited. The neighbors all came to welcome the traveler from afar. The second brother was overcome with shame. Hearing his two little children cry and beg for their mother, alone and desolate, his bowels were torn inch by inch. Those of the village who knew of it all covered their sleeves and laughed. In all matters of respect and compliance, deceit and defiance toward brothers, the retribution of calamity or blessing is tenfold compared with that toward strangers; and toward parents it is a hundredfold. Should one not fear? Should one not take warning?

To be upright is to be firmly unshakable; to transform is to come about of itself. This is what is meant by ‘when one’s person is upright, things are done without giving orders’. To make oneself upright requires much effort; to transform others has many subtle workings. If a man can make himself upright, there is no one he cannot set upright. Because he is upright, all men revere him; and where men feel reverence is where their hearts are transformed. If at that point of transformation one moves them with utmost sincerity, ever so gently, they will of themselves turn at a touch and appear at a lift, and there will be none who do not follow. But if I use my own uprightness to expose another’s crookedness, and reproach him at the slightest occasion, he will not be willing to accept the teaching, and will hotly argue right and wrong — does that not rather crush and cut off his good heart? This is the common failing of those who love goodness in these days: their hand is too heavy, and they cling and will not turn. This should be deeply guarded against. Take care not to forsake your own field to weed another’s. Wang Bao dwelt by the Qi, and the people west of the river became good singers; Mian Ju dwelt at Gaotang, and the people of western Qi became good at song. Did he give each man the measures, and teach them the beat day by day?

In purity, value forbearance; in benevolence, value decisiveness. Do not confer small favors at the cost of the greater whole; do not use public principle to gratify private feeling. When busy, meet it with leisure; when urgent, meet it the more with calm. When there is nothing to do, do not forget to guard and examine yourself; when there is something to do, you must be patient. Do not harbor suspicion out of a settled mind; do not cling to your own view and refuse counsel. When the measure of things is clear, affairs may be lessened; when praise and blame are forgotten, the heart may be cleansed. Uprightness can reach the gods; loyalty and good faith can travel among the barbarous tribes. Only when a man’s character has come to this may one speak of uprightness.

Only after the heart is rectified can one rectify oneself and rectify things. Once the heart is rectified, all things are settled. For the enticements of sound and form that move us from without are a disease of the branches; the arising of deluded feelings within is the disease of the root. One who studies the Way should first govern the inner to withstand the outer, and must not crave the outer to the harm of the inner. Then the heart is rectified and the person established, and there is nothing that does not follow and transform. For when the root of the one heart is strong and full, the branches and leaves of all things are of themselves luxuriant. Therefore to guide others one must first purify the heart; to set others right one must first set oneself right.

Chan Master Yuan of Mount Fu in the Song dynasty said: The mind is the master of the whole body and the root of all practices. If the mind is not subtly awakened, deluded feelings arise of themselves; and once deluded feelings have arisen, principle is not clearly seen, and right and wrong fall into confusion. Therefore in governing the mind one must seek subtle awakening. Awakened, the spirit is harmonious and the temper calm, the countenance reverent and the face grave, and deluded thoughts and emotional cares all melt into the true mind. This is the method of rectifying the heart.

Guo Tai of the Later Han, courtesy name Linzong, once crossed a river with Li Ying, governor of Henan, and those who saw them thought it a boat of immortals. The court repeatedly summoned him, but he would not answer. By nature he was especially discerning of men, and loved to encourage and advance scholars, many of whom he brought to accomplishment. When Mao Rong, sheltering from the rain, sat bolt upright, he urged him to study; when Meng Min, having broken his rice steamer, did not look back, Tai judged him a man of resolve and also urged him to study — and both became famous scholars. He raised Shentu Pan from among the lacquer workers, and recognized Yu Cheng among the gate guards. Of the rest, many who came from butchers, wine sellers, and the ranks of soldiers became renowned through Tai’s encouragement. Zuo Yuan, a student in the commandery school, had been expelled for breaking the law. Tai met him on the road and comforted him, saying: ‘In old days Yan Zhuoju was a great robber of Liangfu, and Duan Ganmu a great horse trader of Jin, yet in the end they became loyal worthies of Qi and Wei. Do not be angry and resentful; reproach yourself, and that is all.’ When someone criticized Tai for not cutting off wicked men, Tai said: ‘If a man is without benevolence, to hate him too much brings disorder.’ Zuo Yuan had been about to gather companions to take revenge, but was stopped by Tai’s teaching. Jia Shu was of a treacherous nature and a scourge to the village. When Tai’s mother died, Jia Shu came to offer condolences, and some thought it strange; Tai said: ‘Confucius did not cut off the people of Huxiang. Ziyuan has washed his heart and turned toward goodness, and so I accept his advance.’ When Shu heard this, he reformed himself into a good man. As for Shi Shubin, Huang Yun, and others, they all had great reputations, but Tai knew they were not genuine and said they would surely fail — and so it proved. When the proscription of the faction broke out, many men of note suffered, but Tai, by concealing evil and proclaiming good, alone escaped the net of the world. When he died, more than a thousand came to his funeral and together carved a stone and set up a monument. Cai Yong said: ‘I have written many epitaphs, but only for Guo Youdao has my writing been without shame.’

Sima Guang of the Song dynasty was loyal, generous, and upright, and his name was known throughout the land. When he dwelt at Luoyang, the customs of the place were wholly changed: all esteemed reputation and integrity, and were ashamed to speak of gain; every man knew to stand in awe of honor and shame. When young men were about to do anything, they would warn one another: ‘Do no evil; Sima Duanming may come to know of it.’

Liu Ju, magistrate of Yongqiu, transformed the people by propriety and righteousness. Whenever litigants came, he would with a gentle face earnestly admonish them, saying: ‘Anger can be endured; the magistrate’s court is a place one should never enter.’ He sent them home to think again, and the litigants, moved to understanding, would each withdraw. The customs of the place were greatly transformed, and the people’s virtue returned to generosity. Now to hear and judge lawsuits is meant for the people’s good; yet there are those who rely too much on the law and do not understand the feelings of those below, and often hold to their course until men die. How much better to be modest and forgiving, and so obtain the true circumstances?

Chen Shi of the Later Han dwelt in his village with an even mind, dealing with things impartially. When there were disputes, men would seek his judgment; he would explain to them where right and wrong lay, and none went away resentful. People said: ‘Better to be punished by the law than to be found wanting by Master Chen.’ Once a thief lodged on a roof beam. Shi rose, took up a candle, and calling his sons and nephews, instructed them, saying: ‘A man must not fail to exhort himself. A wicked man is not necessarily evil by nature; habit becomes second nature, and so he comes to this. The gentleman on the beam is such a one.’ The thief was startled and dropped to the ground, begging forgiveness. Shi gently made him understand, gave him two bolts of silk, and told him to reform himself. His transforming influence reached the whole county, and there was no more thieving.

Empress Wu usurped the Tang. Wu Chengsi and Wu Sansi schemed to be made heir apparent, and the Empress’s mind was not yet settled. Di Renjie, wholly loyal to the Tang house, would calmly speak to the Empress, saying: ‘Emperor Wen braved wind and rain to settle the empire and hand it down to his sons and grandsons. Emperor Gaozong entrusted his two sons to Your Majesty. Now to transfer it to another clan — is that not impermissible? Moreover, between aunt and nephew, and between mother and son, which is nearer? If Your Majesty establishes a son, then after ten thousand years he will be offered sacrifice in the ancestral temple, and the line will continue without end. If you establish a nephew, I have never heard of a nephew who became Son of Heaven and enshrined his aunt in the ancestral temple.’ Thereupon he urged the Empress to recall the Prince of Luling and restore him as heir apparent, and so the Zhou was transformed back into the Tang. He afterward became a Grand Councilor and was enfeoffed as Duke of Liang.

In the Five Dynasties, Fang Jingbo was governor of Qinghe. His mother, of the Cui family, was versed in the classics and of clear understanding. A woman of Beiqiu accused her son of unfilial conduct. The mother said: ‘The people do not yet know propriety and righteousness; how can he be deeply blamed?’ So she summoned the mother, had her sit at the same couch and eat with her, and made the son stand in attendance below the hall to watch Jingbo serving his mother. After ten days the son repented and asked to go home. The mother said: ‘He is ashamed in face, but his heart is not yet changed.’ They kept him more than twenty days longer, until the son knocked his head on the ground till it bled, and his mother, weeping, begged to take him home. Afterward he was known for filial piety.

Shi Zuo and Shi You were brothers, both prefects, who had retired to live at home. Their landed property was unevenly divided, and there was a rift between them like that between lips and teeth. Relatives and friends could not reconcile them. A gentleman of the same district, Mr. Yan Feng of Xiting, was known for filial piety and fraternal love; he served his elder brother as a father, and spared no effort in comforting and protecting him. Once, in the same boat with Shi You, he spoke of the property matter. Yan knitted his brows and said to him: ‘My elder brother is weak, and that is just what troubles me. If he had the strength of your elder brother, and could take all my land by force, what would I have to worry about?’ And he wept without stopping. Shi You was moved to compassion and understanding. He then invited Yan to go with him to his brother’s house, where he bowed and wept, deeply reproaching himself, while Shi Zuo too wept and comforted him, and each wished to yield the land to the other; so they loved each other as brothers to the end of their lives. To this day the two families flourish, and men still delight to tell the story. The three cases above — loyalty, filial piety, and fraternal love — are those who transformed others. Their root was simply that they made themselves good, and men were moved and transformed accordingly. That human nature is good is here the more clearly seen.

Yu Tieqiao said: To be orphaned or widowed is the misfortune of a life; to be old or young is what every life must pass through. To pity and relieve, to respect and cherish, is likewise the conscience stirred of itself. Unless a man be the worst villain under heaven, there is none who takes pleasure in oppressing the orphan, hounding the widow, insulting the aged, or cheating the young. Yet King Wen’s government said no more than ‘Have pity on these solitary ones’; and the Master’s aspiration said no more than ‘the old at ease, the young cherished’. Why is this? A good heart is easily stirred, but the measure of goodness is hard to fill. Those without means should indeed do all their hearts can; those with means should practically and concretely carry out the work of pity and relief, and warmly and truly accomplish the task of respect and cherishing — they must not merely ease their conscience in their own breast. The poem of Bai Juyi, the Grand Tutor, says: ‘In the round of the year, spring days are few; in this world, the suffering are many.’ And again: ‘The nature of things is a little to be pitied; the heart of man grows tender with age.’ The words of a benevolent man are gentle to read.

The orphan is one who has not yet come to accomplishment, while his parents have already passed away — perhaps his mother died and his father has just remarried, or his father died and his mother is considering another marriage; or worse, both parents are gone, and he stands alone, small and helpless. Unfortunate to this degree, how can his lot be borne? Even a passerby feels compassion; how much more one of his own clan and kin, who can hardly look on unmoved. To pity is to grieve for him. One should with utmost sincerity grieve for him, nourish him, and teach him, so that where he had no one to lean on he has someone, and where he had no support he has support, until he is brought to accomplishment. Thus one plants thick virtue among men and comforts the hidden spirits below the earth — and the reward is surely not small.
Appendix: The Method of the Foundling Bureau

In the Great Song, the prefectures and counties established Foundling Bureaus. Whenever a poor family had a child it was willing to rear, the child was sent to the bureau and placed with a wet nurse to be brought up; or those who had no children of their own came to the bureau to take one. Even in years of famine none were abandoned. Such was the fullness of the Song government’s care for orphans. And now benevolence has spread wide and many love goodness: in the capital, Yangzhou, Suzhou, and elsewhere, Foundling Halls have been built, and their method is even more thorough. Funds are gathered and a large empty house is bought, with high walls on all four sides. Within the hall, beds, stoves, and all things needed for food and use are complete. In front a small door is set, kept bolted, and no man may enter; an elderly, strict, and firm man is chosen to guard it. Poor women who are stout and healthy and have children of their own, and are willing to serve as wet nurses, are brought with their children to live inside, and are given wages and food according to measure. Outside the door a large drum is hung. When a child is born that the parents do not wish to raise, they place it in a basket, write down its surname and the year, month, and day of its birth, and stick a paper label on the basket. Waiting until nightfall, when no one is about, they carry it to the gate, set the child on the ground, and strike the drum once. Hearing the drum, someone comes out from the hall and takes the child in; by then the one who brought it has gone — for fear that the person might be ashamed, or afraid of trouble, and would not wish to be seen. When the child arrives, the wet nurse becomes its mother, and it is called by her surname, lest in time it be forgotten, or, being many, be mistaken. An experienced physician for children is engaged to examine and treat illnesses. A charity burial ground is provided: if any die young, they are coffined and buried there. Two or three diligent women are hired besides: when a child is weaned, they are set to care for it, and one woman can care for several children, so as to make room for those who come later. When a wet nurse’s milk fails and she leaves the hall, if she loves the child she nursed, she may take it with her. When a child is five or six years old, it is taught according to the quality of its nature. Outside the hall another elementary school is set up, and one teacher engaged. Boys of fine intelligence are taught to read; the dull and slow are set to sweeping and sprinkling in the hall and the school. Girls of good appearance are guided by the wet nurses in household matters and taught needlework; the simple and clumsy are likewise set to work. Boys over ten are not permitted to enter the hall again — this is to keep them far from suspicion. Some are adopted as heirs by the childless; some are given to monks or Daoists as incense boys; some are placed with prosperous families in service. Each is sent out according to his ability and lodged according to circumstance; no price is taken for their persons, and there is no fear that they will be left with nowhere to go. Though they be of the lowest station, it is still better than to die young. And if one is of uncommon gifts, in after days he will make his own way — that is not the responsibility of the master of the foundling hall. If one grows up and can make his own living and establish a household, he may take a girl from the hall as his wife, and is taught not to marry into another surname, to show that he does not forget his origin. Girls are not to leave the hall before they are of age to pin up their hair; once of age, they are married to common townsfolk, the betrothal money being enough for a little clothing and ornament, and any surplus going to the hall’s common funds. They may not be married into the gentry families, nor sold as bondmaids, since the good or base origin of their birth cannot be known. If any is beautiful and a rich family wishes to take her as a concubine, this is refused; it does no harm to righteousness. Do not say that one may take a larger betrothal gift for the hall’s public expenses. Among the faithful donors, one who is loyal, upright, clear-sighted, experienced in affairs, and has much leisure is chosen to oversee the whole. All the going out of men and women, the coming in of money, and every small daily matter is examined and checked. A chest is placed at the gate, so that passersby of good will may set down a coin or a handful of rice, all of which is recorded. Once the framework is complete, good connections gradually widen, and if it is carried on long, it need not be abandoned. This is a great good that stands alongside Heaven and Earth. What is difficult is the gathering of funds. But in a large prefecture there are many abandoned infants, so the expense is great — yet the faithful donors are many too. In a small prefecture the donors are few, so the abandoned infants are few, and the expense is small as well. The hearts of those who love goodness are the same everywhere; if two or three take the lead, there is no place where it cannot be done. The world need not fear that there are no men of means; it need only fear that there are no men who can make the great vow. Therefore I have set this out in detail, for those who love goodness to choose and adopt.

Ye Mengde of the Song dynasty said: When I was at Xuchang, there was a great flood that year, and countless people died of starvation. I memorialized the throne and opened the ever-normal granaries for relief, and more than a hundred thousand lives were saved. Only there was no way to rescue the abandoned children. I happened to ask those about me who had no sons why they did not take and rear them. They said: ‘There are quite a few who want a child; the trouble is that when the harvest is good and the child grows up, the parents come to claim him.’ So I devised a rule: in every case of a small child abandoned because of disaster, the parents should not be allowed to take it back. I then had several thousand blank certificates made and issued inside and outside the city; whoever took a child stated where it came from, which was written plainly on the certificate, and a rough register was kept. Those who took in many were rewarded, and the surplus grain of the ever-normal granary was shared out to provide means for the poor. When the matter was settled the certificates were checked: there were three thousand eight hundred persons in all. This too is what those who govern the people ought to know. Again, since the wars began, there were those who hid in the forests and marshes, and many were discovered by the crying of their children and did not escape harm. Hence those fleeing the bandits generally abandoned their infants without a look. Someone taught them to make a ball of cotton wool and put it in the child’s mouth, filling it fairly full without stopping the breath, and to keep a little powdered licorice, dipping it in water when tying it so that the child might taste its flavor. With this in its mouth the child makes no sound of itself, and the soft wool does not hurt its mouth. So a block was carved and posted along the roads, and very many infants were saved alive. This too is what those who meet with upheaval ought to know.

Zhang Xiaoji of the Song dynasty was the son-in-law of a rich man of the same commandery. The rich man had a son who was unworthy, and drove him out of the house. When the rich man fell ill and was near death, he entrusted the whole family property to Xiaoji. Later the rich man’s son became a beggar. Xiaoji pitied him in his loneliness and asked him: ‘Can you tend a garden?’ He said: ‘If I could get food by it, I should be more than glad.’ So he took him in. After a while he asked again: ‘Can you manage a storehouse?’ He said: ‘Tending the garden was already a blessing; to manage a storehouse would be a greater blessing still.’ So he set him to manage the storehouse. Xiaoji observed the man: he was careful and honest, with none of his old ways. He then handed over the whole family property to him. After Xiaoji died, a friend of his was traveling in the Song Mountains when he met on the road a retinue of banners and outriders like that of a great official. Peering at the one in the carriage, he saw it was Xiaoji. They bowed to each other, and the friend asked how it was. Xiaoji said: ‘The Lord on High, because I returned the property and did not cheat the orphan, appointed me master of this mountain.’ With that he vanished.

In the time of the Zhou there was the Righteous Aunt of Lu, a wife of Lu. When the men of Qi attacked Lu, the Righteous Aunt abandoned the child she was carrying in her arms and carried the one she was leading by the hand. The Qi soldiers asked her: ‘Who is the one you abandoned?’ The woman said: ‘My own son.’ They asked again: ‘Who is the one you carry?’ The woman said: ‘My elder brother’s son.’ The soldiers said: ‘Why do you abandon your own child and carry your brother’s son?’ She answered: ‘A son is a private love to his mother; a nephew’s following his aunt is a public duty. To turn from the public to the private and so cut off my brother’s orphan — that I will not do.’ The Qi soldiers said: ‘In the countryside of Lu even a woman holds fast to duty — how much more its ruler?’ They turned their army about and withdrew. When the ruler of Lu heard of it, he bestowed rolls of silk on her and gave her the title of Righteous Aunt. This woman of Lu preserved an orphan, and by one speech kept the state safe. Yet men today who are called bearded males turn their backs on righteousness and snatch at life — can they feel no shame before her?

Zhang Yi of Shu-Han was a friend of Yang Gong from youth. When Gong died, his orphan was not yet a few years old. Yi brought Gong’s mother to his own house and served her, found a wife for Gong’s son, and bought fields and a house for him. Men esteemed his righteousness. He afterward became governor of Yizhou.

Shen Jiamo of Wujiang, while his father was an official of the Yellow Gate, dwelt in his village as a lover of righteousness. In the same district there was a certain Master Gu, barely ten years old, who had lost his father though his family was fairly well off. At that time there was alarm of bandits, and the county magistrate assembled the great families to discuss contribution to the army’s provisions, and the assembly said there was none like young Gu. Master Shen alone said with a sigh: ‘This small orphan — how can he bear such a levy?’ The others said that his servants were many and could be put to the task. Shen said: ‘It is precisely those overbearing servants I fear: they would use the heavy levy to bully the young master, and his house would be ruined at once. If Gu must be levied, I am willing to take his place.’ And he gladly wrote down his own name. For several years of war, young Gu was never burdened, and the whole district praised his righteousness.

The widow — she is in the prime of her years when her husband is suddenly taken; she is a single form with a single shadow, and nothing meets her eye but emptiness — how much worse if her daughters are young and her sons small, and a hundred matters are left undone! This is what Mencius meant by ‘poor and with none to whom to appeal’. Poor means utterly at the end: with calamity such as this, is she not at the extremity? To whom shall she speak? To relieve her is to sustain and support her, to nourish her person and complete her chastity. Among those born between heaven and earth, none is more bitterly placed than a widow: if young, she is bullied by the violent; if rich, she is devoured by the clan; if old, she is doddering, and who pities her; if poor, she has no means for food or clothing. And a widow with no son who resolves to keep her chastity is rarer still. If a man can pity and relieve her, he can move the Lord on High in the highest heaven and stir gods and spirits in the three realms — how can this be called a small kindness?

Du Huan of Jinling in the Ming dynasty: his father Du Yiyuan was a friend of Chang Yungong. When Gong died, his mother, old and with nowhere to go, came through the rain to Huan’s house. By then Yiyuan was dead. Huan asked in amazement what had happened, and the old woman told him through her tears. Huan too wept, helped her to a seat and bowed to her, and ordered the family to serve her as their own grandmother. The old woman was narrow and quick-tempered, and at the least displeasure would scold and rage; Huan went along with her and served her the more respectfully. When she fell ill, he attended her with soup and medicine himself. At her death she said: ‘I have burdened Master Du; may the sons and grandsons of Master Du all be like him.’ When she died, he buried her with full ceremony and sacrificed at her grave on the seasonal festivals. People praised his high righteousness.

Zhu Hui of Nanyang and Zhang Kan were of the same county — the Zhang Kan of whom it was said, ‘While Master Zhang governs, we cannot contain our joy.’ Kan met Hui in the Imperial Academy and treated him with the affection of a friend, grasping his arm and saying: ‘When one day I leave the world, I would entrust my wife and children to you, brother.’ Hui, because Kan was his senior, did not dare to answer. Thereafter they did not meet again. After Zhang’s death, Hui heard that his wife and children were in poverty, and shared his own food and clothing with them. Hui’s son was puzzled and asked: ‘Father, you were not friends with Master Zhang, so why suddenly do this?’ Hui said: ‘Kan once spoke to me as to a true friend; I have kept it in my heart.’ Hui afterward governed Linhuai, where he also had good administration, and the people sang of him. He rose to be a Director of the Secretariat. Now the orphaned and widowed with none to depend on are everywhere; how can we have them all cared for like these several gentlemen? Therefore I urge those of good will to follow this example and found charitable societies for the relief of widows. The method is to gather friends who will contribute money, collected monthly or yearly, kept in the hands of those of means, and to have them seek out the widowed and poor and give them a fixed sum each month. This is indeed a boundless hidden merit. Those who cannot do this may, when they see or hear of such cases, relieve them according to their means — is this not benevolence too? Yet I fear that those who have such a heart are ever checked by suspicion and slander. The wise should think how to manage it by good means.

Duke Zhao Kangjing of the Song dynasty was orphaned at seven. His mother, with firm resolve, taught him diligently, and he afterward passed the examinations and became a Hanlin Academician. Zhao asked that his mother be granted an honorary title, and the Chancellor said: ‘Your grand enfeoffment is not far off.’ Zhao said: ‘My widowed mother is eighty-two, and cannot be counted on from morning to evening. I would have her enjoy the honor while she may.’ The Chancellor assented. And Li Yun was orphaned at three; someone tried to persuade his mother to remarry. She angrily rebuked him, saying: ‘The bond of husband and wife belongs to the natural relations; life and death are ordained by the true Lord. I would sooner starve than marry again.’ So she set her mind firmly on keeping her chastity and taught her son, who passed the examinations. Alas, such a woman is revered by the gods and respected by men, and her reward must be great, for she honored the human relations — how could it stop at her son’s advancement? That a widow must not be slighted is indeed so; yet this is taught again here because I would have every widow know what to follow and stand on her own feet. And those who are orphaned must not give themselves up either. They should remember that many who were orphaned became great vessels: Zhang Shixun, poor and orphaned, by bitter resolve rose to the position of a chief councilor; Lü Hui, orphaned though of good family, cultivated himself in secret and became a famous censor, and men only then knew he was the grandson of Duke Lü Hui. Others such as Liu Zhi, Ouyang Xiu, and Chen Yaozuo all studied hard in youth and rose to be Grand Councilors. Only thus can one somewhat repay the frost and snow of a widowed mother’s bitterness. I urge and exhort once again; my meaning is most earnest.

The old are those of advanced years, who have seen much of the world and passed through many affairs. To respect them is to apply sincerity, to express love, and to provide for their ease in every way. Even to dare not slight them in a single thought or a single matter is also respect. Longevity stands first among the five blessings, and age draws near to fatherhood; such a man must have planted roots in a former life, and be one who in this life is willing to accumulate virtue. Moreover he is practiced in all affairs and can serve as a model; the benefit to be drawn from him is not small. How can he be slighted? But men of the world, because the aged are dim and doddering, either loathe them or insult them; who is willing to be careful and reverent? They do not know the saying: ‘Respect the old, and you shall yourself grow old.’ Yang Danian took first place in the examinations at twenty, and was in the palace secretariat with Zhou Han and Zhu Ang, both of them old men, and Yang slighted and mocked them. Zhou said: ‘Do not mock my age, sir; old age will come round to you in the end.’ Ang shook his head and said: ‘Do not — do not; you will only be mocked by others.’ Yang indeed died in his prime. I would have the frivolous young men of today read this case and change their ways at once, restoring generosity of heart. Whenever they meet an old man, let them hold an even mind, not asking whether he be rich or poor, noble or base, but make a point of carrying within them a measure of love and respect — then hoary head and bushy brows will one day be their own portion too.

The Taizu Emperor instructed the Ministry of Rites, saying: ‘To honor age is to teach reverence; to serve one’s elders is to teach obedience. Under Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou, none failed to honor age. The rites of supporting the aged were in truth never abolished, and therefore men rose up in filial and fraternal conduct, customs were simple and generous, and the way of government flourished in peace. Do you proclaim my command and renew it.’

The Avatamsaka Sutra says: ‘May all living beings bring forth the bodhi mind and be complete in wisdom, preserving life forever without end. May all living beings be complete in the practice of the dharma that transcends old age and death, so that no calamity or poison may harm their lives. May all living beings be complete in accomplishing a body free of illness and affliction, with the power to live as long as they wish and dwell as they please. May all living beings attain freedom from old age and sickness, abide always in the root of life, advance with courage and vigor, and enter the Buddha’s wisdom.’ From this we see that the aged are like the sun’s shadow caught on the mountain: their time is limited. If they do not practice with the utmost urgency, what will they have to support their journey to the West?

Wang Bin was sickly and thin in youth, and judged that his own life would not be long. Whenever he saw an old man he would respect and envy him; when any passed his gate, even of the meanest sort, he would stand up, and in walking he would always give way. Afterward his illness gradually healed, his strength grew greater, and he lived to ninety-three.

In the Sui dynasty there was a monk over a hundred years old who deeply understood the wondrous meaning of the Lotus Sutra. He once told the assembly: ‘I, poor monk, respect the aged as my parents and serve them as bodhisattvas. Whatever I could put my strength to, I never failed to do with all my heart. That in this life I have penetrated the Buddha’s dharma and enjoyed long years is all due to respecting the aged. You, the great assembly, must not slight the old and so diminish your blessing and longevity.’ Now in the field of fame and gain, a finger-snap and it is past; one should rather work on one’s own portion. Otherwise one comes to the world in vain and makes a wasted journey, missing all the Buddhas’ words — ‘May my life be long, that I may diligently practice every good’; ‘May my blessing and virtue be abundant, that I may broadly benefit all beings.’ Alas, alas, young men! They know only to rely on their talents and to slight their elders, not knowing that long life is given by Heaven and age is honored by kings. Though one have much talent, such a state is hard to reach.

In the Song dynasty, in the household of Wu Yuansi, there were eight persons of eighty, ninety, and a hundred years or more. The emperor asked what had brought this about: it was that for generations the family had kept together in righteousness and never divided. The throne conferred a plaque on their gate and granted them exceptional favors. Now when we consider the establishment of the schools for elders, it existed already in the time of Yao and Shun, and the three dynasties revered and honored the institution, recording it in detail in the Book of Rites and other works. When the Master spoke of his aspiration, he too said, ‘the old at ease’. Thus both the statutes of the state and the hearts of scholars and people have their part in it. Can one say that the aged of others have nothing to do with me, and not respect them?

The young are children, ignorant and without knowledge. To cherish does not mean only to love them; it means to hold them in one’s bosom. For those who are their elders, to protect the innocent and cherish the young is the natural order of things. How much more when there are those whose lot is hard and whose distress is pitiable — a son by a former wife, a younger brother by another mother, the child of a concubine or bondmaid. If one uses one’s seniority to oppress them, and the solitary and the innocent are made to suffer cruelty, who could be more pitiable? Extending this broadly, wherever there are young people, and among servants and menials, one should with special care pity them; one should not make distinctions between mine and yours. As for scheming to swallow up the family property, then elders, elder brothers and sisters, and husbands who have married into the house are often unkind and unrighteous, oppressing the young and lowly, even to the point of cleverly framing complaints, forging contracts, instructing brokers to give false testimony, and bribing clerks to twist the documents, so that the victims have no one to appeal to. There are even those who by secret plots destroy their lives. In old days the household of Li Zhiben had more than a hundred sons and grandsons, elders and young in harmony; the brothers Yang Cheng depended on one another in their orphaned loneliness. The hearts of our forebears were like this, and truly they are worthy of imitation.

When Yuan Dexiu of the Tang was poor, his elder brother died young, leaving an orphan only a month old, and his brother’s wife died too, so there was no milk to nurse the child. Dexiu wept aloud day and night, holding his brother’s child, and put it to his own breast; within ten days milk came. The child was thus brought up. Such a thing is but a chance occurrence, yet in it one may see that to cherish the young accords with the heart of Heaven. Confucius said: ‘The young, cherish them.’ Mencius said: ‘Treat your own young as young, and extend it to the young of others.’ The sages’ instructions could go no further. Why do elders not take them to heart?

When Liu Yi was in Chuzhou, the people were starving and abandoned their children. Yi issued a proclamation calling on people to take and rear them, giving two pints of grain from the Guanghui Granary each day, and each day he had the children brought to the government office to be inspected. The common people, taking profit from the two pints, all raised them, and those saved were beyond counting. Now the way to relieve famine lies first in taking in and rearing the orphaned young, drawing them out of the ditches and placing them in swaddling clothes. Those who govern the people should make this their first concern; its hidden merit exceeds that of saving grown men.

Yang Zhu of the Ming was kind and generous by nature. He bought a donkey for going to court. A neighbor, old and newly given a son, found that the donkey’s braying frightened the child, so Yang sold it and walked to court. Later, when he was living at home, a farmer knocked over his family gravestone, and the grave keeper came running to report it. He asked: ‘Did it hurt the child?’ They said no. He said joyfully: ‘That is fortunate. Tell that family to take good care of the child and not frighten him.’ Yang’s great virtues were many, but even in these two matters men find it hard to equal him. It is fitting that from orphaned poverty he rose to eminence.

Kun means ‘multitude’, and refers to all insects great and small. Since even these may not be injured, we may know what is to be done with what is weightier and greater. Men today wantonly take the lives of living things, not knowing that creeping things that breathe all have the Buddha-nature. ‘Do not break what is growing’ — the Confucian teaching is clear. How can one say that insects are mere trifles, and that plants and trees have no awareness, and so injure them at a stroke?

The preface to the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: Whatever has blood and breath must have awareness; whatever has awareness must share one substance. The Surangama Sutra says: The Tathagata has always taught that all things that arise are manifested by the mind alone; all causes and effects, worlds and motes of dust, take their substance from the mind. Among them, even a blade of grass or a knotted thread — inquire into its root and origin, and all have their own substance and nature. Again, when Master Sheng preached, the stones of the mountain nodded. Can walls and tiles be said to have no Buddha-nature? Or again, the redbud of the Tian family, and the auspicious willow of the Tang Secretariat: at the end of the Jianzhong era, when Yao Lingyan’s troops mutinied and the imperial carriage went out to Fengtian, the tree withered and died; in the first year of Xingyuan, when the carriage returned, the tree flourished again. Can plants and trees then be called unaware? The Most High’s meaning in handing down this warning is to show men how, toward all beings with feeling and without, to nurture everywhere a single heart of compassion and a single breast of living kindness.

When the Tathagata was preaching the dharma, a clam, rejoicing, leaped out upon the bank and listened with all its heart. By chance it was killed by the staff of one of those listening to the teaching. Because it had heard the dharma, after its death it was born in the Trayastrimsa Heaven and became its lord. From that heaven it came again to where the Buddha was, heard the wondrous meaning, and by that awakening realized the fruit of srotapanna. The clam is a very small creature, yet afterward it realized a very great fruit. Seen in this light, may insects be injured?

Formerly there was a monk whose eye of the Way was not yet clear, and who received the offerings of Jingde and his son in vain. After his death he was born as a mushroom in Jingde’s garden, and day by day furnished vegetables for that household; when others wished to pick it, they could not find it. The mushroom is a very small thing, yet it had this extraordinary connection. Seen in this light, may plants and trees be injured?

Han Shineng of Changzhou in the Ming dynasty lived for generations at Lumu and was very poor. His grandfather Yongchun would rise early every day and, broom in hand, sweep the river snails from the two banks back into midstream, to save them from the fishermen. Hungry as he was, he would sweep for several li. In the dingmao year of the Longqing era, Shineng went to the provincial examinations; he was then forty. His father Zongdao, reflecting that his own father had labored so diligently to save lives, and that his son was now grown and still without advancement, thought: ‘Now that I happen to have ten pieces of silver, why not buy living creatures and set them free to pray for his blessing?’ Early in the morning he bought a great turtle and a great red carp and released them. That night he dreamed that a spirit told him: ‘Your father’s merit is great, and your son shall pass the examinations. Now that you have ransomed and released a divine turtle and a divine carp, your son shall enter the Hanlin Academy and rise to the first rank.’ In the event he passed, went on from one success to the next, entered the Hanlin, and rose to be Vice Minister. He was sent as envoy to Korea and was granted the robe of the first rank.

A certain woman of Hangzhou was fierce and violent by nature. When ants crawled along her kitchen stove she burned them with fire, and those that died were beyond counting. She also used to stop up earthworm holes with lime. She bore a son, still in arms. One day, when she had gone out and returned, she saw a black mass on the bed; looking in terror, she saw it was her son, already bitten to death by a swarm of ants. Grieving for the child, she too died suddenly.

Wu Yi of Taicang prefecture dreamed one night of two men in green begging for their lives. Waking, he said: ‘There must be some creature about to die.’ At dawn he went out to the gate to watch, and saw several men coming with axes and saws: they had bought two ginkgo trees and were coming to cut them down. Yi understood, paid them the price, and the trees were spared.

Emperor Zhezong of the Song once broke off willow branches at play in the palace. Cheng Yi said: ‘In spring, when things are growing, they must not be broken without cause.’ The emperor was pleased and followed his advice. Cheng Yi congratulated him, saying: ‘If Your Majesty extends this heart to the whole empire, the essential way of a sovereign is all contained in it.’ Again, it is told that Gao Zigao would not break anything while it was growing, and that Zhou Lianxi would not cut the grass in his courtyard, saying that he wished to be of one mind with his own living growth. All these show the sages and worthies keeping a heart of benevolence and not slighting the small and minute.

Chen Jianfu said: The benevolent man gives away his unused surplus, and the wise man bestows a great virtue that seeks no return, so that creatures whose bowels are cut and whose breath is failing may have their lives extended at the very edge of the blade, and withered spirits and frightened souls may be brought back to life above the cauldron. Such merit may be divided thus: there are three kinds of ‘no fixed rule’ in releasing life, and two kinds in which release is not required. There is releasing life for creatures, releasing life for people, and releasing life for oneself. Now men of the world who release living creatures mostly fix on set days and hours, and those who seek profit thereupon spread their nets and arrows to meet them, so that many perish of exhaustion — this is to use killing as a way of releasing. If in the streets and markets, wherever eye and ear reach, one buys and releases as occasion offers, this is called releasing without fixed times. Men of the world dig ponds and set up enclosures; since there is a fixed place, others can lie in wait there, and the creature that has just escaped the fisherman’s net becomes the cook’s soup — this is to use releasing as a way of killing. But in rivers and lakes, in woods and marshes, wherever the ground is suitable, with trustworthy men to oversee it and going suddenly without warning, this is called releasing without a fixed place. Men of the world release living creatures outside, yet at home slaughter without misgiving, saying even that domestic animals are kept for man and it is their lot to furnish food; they do not know that sons and grandsons are also raised and tended, and if they were butchered and eaten at will, how would that feel to them? The proverb says: ‘To manage one’s affairs and pay one’s debts is better than to give alms; to form societies for releasing life — how does it compare with simply abstaining from killing?’ So too, grass and trees are all living beings, and lice and moths all have the Buddha-nature. Some break down walls and destroy hibernating creatures; some overturn nests and smash eggs; some leave rotting meat to gather ants, or let standing water breed maggots; some keep rare fish and birds and procure living things to feed them. Though I have no mind to kill, the creature has a way to die — all such things should be avoided and guarded against beforehand, for their lives’ sake. This is called releasing without releasing, and releasing without a fixed object. As for those that have been bitten or caught in nets, and if released may not live, they should rather be tended and nursed until they recover; and if they cannot be saved whole, then bury them. Again, there are fierce beasts, poisonous fish, noxious insects, and birds of prey: to save the life of one such is in fact to prolong poison for many. In such cases one should weigh the many against the few that are saved, and measure the weight of merit and fault, and let them live and die of themselves, as though one had neither seen nor heard them. These two kinds need not be released. In all such matters, follow circumstance and follow your strength, suit the occasion and what is fitting. Do not think that to kill a small creature does no harm; do not think that to release a small creature does no good. Do not, for fear of trouble, check a thought of goodness; do not, for haggling over price, break off a good connection. One creature is not few; many beings are not many. The tiny winged things are not small; horses and oxen are not great. One coin is not too little; ten thousand strings are not too much. What is called ‘releasing life for creatures’ is exhausted in these words. As with creatures, so with men. Some have fallen into error and are to be pitied; some are wronged and trapped with no one to save them; some are beset by robbers, by flood or fire; some fall into illness and mortal danger; some, having failed in their pursuits, lose the wish to live; some, unable to repay their debts, wish to die. If one can supply them with means, open a way of life for them, lend them help and turn the matter about, and contrive their release — this is ‘releasing life for people’, and it concerns us even more nearly than the release of creatures. Therefore, if one recalls how in one’s own distress one longed to be saved, one’s body and another’s are naturally not divided; and if one extends the heart that is grateful for rescue, merit and virtue naturally find their home. As for ‘releasing life for oneself’, this is doubly urgent. Where men crave life, there they can lose it; to lay down killing is therefore to live long. If one can let the six periods of the day polish one, and penetrate all things, directly recognize the original nature, and clearly attain the unborn, then one cuts the net of worldly truth, removes the shackles of defilement, and becomes one free flowing line, tied neither to coming nor going, unconstrained and unhurried, at ease and at liberty. Planting the mind outside the shell of release, the true mind escapes that turning wheel — then one is neither man nor creature, but rises above the four kinds of birth; with no virtue and no merit, one forever transcends the rewards of blessing. Therefore I append a verse. The verse says: All births bring sorrow in their train; where life is born, release must bear its name. Come, break the cage and soar away: to wake to the unborn is release, I say.

The word ‘fitting’ governs the whole passage down to the sentence ‘and does not afterward regret it’. ‘Ill’ means the ill of wickedness, and also the ill of calamity. To pity is to bend every effort to counsel and guide a man, so that he changes his ways and follows goodness; it is also to arrange matters so that he is safe and each is settled in his proper place — not merely to show a fond and soft compassion. He Longtu said: Whenever evil is first committed, it comes only of a single mistaken thought, and it is not necessarily beyond counsel and restraint. Once evil has been committed, there still remains one thought of clarity, and it is not necessarily beyond rescue. Yet the world often repels such men as though they were enemies, and they rush to death like ducks to the water, so that even if they wish to renew themselves they cannot. Alas!

The Daodejing says: The sage is always good at saving men, and so he wastes no man; always good at saving creatures, and so he wastes no creature. Therefore the good man is the teacher of the bad, and the bad man is the material of the good. If one does not honor his teacher nor cherish his material, though he be clever he is greatly deluded. The Book of Changes says: The sage completes all things by indirect means and leaves nothing behind. The Book of Rites says: Wind and rain, dew and thunder are all nothing but the highest teaching. The frost and the snow: the vast heaven does not mean to harm creatures, but thereby to nourish the source of life and growth. To reprove and to govern: the sage does not mean to make men suffer, but thereby to open the road of self-renewal — all because he would have men turn from evil to good, and so fulfill the embrace that makes all things one body.

Goodness is what all men, self and others alike, may attain. Yet men constantly make a vain division between self and others: the high-minded wish only that goodness should come from themselves, and the low-minded will not have goodness come from others. Some even slander to defame another’s slight fault, or plot in secret to ruin his good name, doing nothing but corrupting their own hearts — what loss is it to him? They do not know that when another has a good thought or a good deed, if I can encourage, praise, and proclaim it, so that his measure is rounded out to fullness and his practice made complete, then his goodness is my goodness, and it is merit without end.

Of the gates of all goodness by which one passes from the ordinary to the sagely, the bringing forth of the bodhi mind is foremost. The bodhi mind is like a seed, for it can bring forth every good dharma; like good soil, for it can grow the pure dharmas of living beings; like pure water, for it can wash away every stain of affliction; like a great fire, for it can burn up all the firewood of wrong views. The Nirvana Sutra says: The Buddha taught that to cultivate one good heart breaks a hundred kinds of evil, as a little fire can burn everything. Thus we know that all goodness is born from a single thought of delight, and appears as the whole body of a good heart, perfecting the wondrous fruit of bodhi, of everlasting joy.

Lei Shu was generous and able to bear with others. When men met him with violence and perversity, he pitied their folly instead, and would always endure and not contend, and so transformed them. Though he suffered great wrongs, he never once brought a man to court. His descendant of the eleventh generation, Lei Fu, became Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent.

Yu Lingyi caught a thief by night and found it was his neighbor’s son. Lingyi said: ‘You were driven to it by poverty, that is all. Here are ten thousand coins to give you a living; do not do wrong again.’ When the man had gone, he called him back and said: ‘You are poor, and carrying money home at night, you may be questioned by the patrol.’ He kept him until dawn and then sent him away, and never spoke of it to anyone. Afterward his sons and grandsons in succession became presented scholars. Men said it was the reward of pitying the wicked.
